title: Resist the beginnings (I.13)
hook: temptations are easiest to overcome at the start
tomorrow: so why put up with someone's worst habit?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the slow plan: root out one fault a year, and push hardest at the start. The line was one a year. Today, the start itself gets a whole chapter.

A phone glows on a nightstand at 11:52. A stranger's post, and one thought knocks: what an idiot. A minute later the thought has a picture, the perfect reply, sharp enough to sting. Then it starts to feel good, warm, almost fun. Thumbs moving now. Three sentences. A fourth. Nobody decided any of this. It walked in one step at a time, and now it's sitting at the kitchen table with its shoes off. So where, exactly, could it have been stopped?
screen: `11:52, ONE THOUGHT KNOCKS.` → `A PICTURE, THEN THE PLEASURE.` → `WHERE COULD IT HAVE BEEN STOPPED?`

segments.voice: The Imitation's answer: at the door. Chapter thirteen of book one starts honestly. As long as we live, it says, trouble and temptation come with life, and it leans on Job, in the Douay-Rheims: "The life of man upon earth is a warfare." No religious order so holy, no place so hidden, that temptation can't reach it. Then comes the map, the part worth keeping. First a plain thought comes to mind. Then a strong picture. Then delight. Then a wrong movement. Then consent. At each step the enemy gets further in, because he wasn't met at the start. It's an honest little map of the inside of a person. So watch most at the beginning, the book says: an enemy is beaten more easily if he's never let through the door of the mind, but met outside the moment he knocks. Here's one to tell a friend tonight. To make the point, this book of devotion borrows a line from a Roman poet. Principiis obsta, resist the beginnings, comes from Ovid's Remedies for Love, advice for getting over someone. A monk's handbook and a love poet agree: once the trouble has grown strong, the cure comes late. And the chapter isn't grim. Temptations, it says, can humble a person, cleanse them and teach them. Nobody is expected to never hear a knock. Just to answer it early.
screen: `THE LIFE OF MAN IS A WARFARE.` · `THOUGHT, PICTURE, DELIGHT, CONSENT.` · `MEET IT AT THE DOOR.` · `A LINE FROM A LOVE POET.` · then, large: `RESIST THE BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let your mind run for a moment. When a pull shows up, a craving, a grudge, the itch to check your phone, catch it at the first step, while it's only a thought, and let it knock without opening. If you pray, you can turn to God right there at the threshold.
Resist the beginnings. The Imitation's counsel for temptation: meet it at the door, while it's still only a thought.
The line to keep: at the start, when it's still a knock and not a guest. Good night.

notes: Imitation I.13 paraphrased: while we live in the world we cannot be without tribulation and temptation (citing Job); no order so holy nor place so secret that there are no temptations; temptations are useful, humbling, cleansing and instructing; watch especially at the beginning, for the enemy is more easily overcome if not suffered to enter the door of the mind but met at the threshold as soon as he knocks; 'principiis obsta: sero medicina paratur'; first a simple thought, then strong imagination, then delight, evil motion and assent. Confirm.
Job 7:1 Douay-Rheims: 'The life of man upon earth is a warfare, and his days are like the days of a hireling.' Only the first clause is quoted. Confirm wording.

v3: 'Principiis obsta' is now credited to Ovid, Remedia Amoris 91 (cited); the Imitation quotes it without naming him. 'Advice for getting over someone' describes the Remedia's subject. Confirm. Original pronunciation is ecclesiastical.
The 'five steps' in the voice are the chapter's own sequence (thought, imagination, delight, motion, assent); the voice lists them without stating a count.

The Imitation is paraphrased throughout (quoted: null): the outline names Benham's translation, which is not on the validator's public-domain list. Confirm each paraphrase against the Latin or Benham.
